chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 9 — The Marks of a Good Government
paragraphs: The question “What absolutely is the best government?” is unanswerable, as well as undefined; or rather, there are as many good answers as there are possible combinations of the absolute and relative situations of all nations.
But if we ask by what sign we can know whether a given people is well or badly governed, that is another matter, and the question, being one of fact, admits of an answer.

It is not, however, answered, because everyone wants to answer it in his own way. Subjects extol public tranquility, citizens individual liberty; one class prefers security of possessions, the other security of person; one regards as best that government which is most severe, the other holds that the mildest is best; one wants crimes punished, the other wants them prevented; one wants the State to be feared by its neighbors, the other prefers that it be ignored; one is content if money circulates, the other demands that the people have bread. Even if we were to agree on these and similar points, would we have made any progress? Since moral qualities do not admit of exact measurement, agreement about the mark does not mean agreement about the measure.

For my part, I am continually astonished that so simple a mark is not recognized, or that men are in such bad faith as not to admit it. What is the end of political association? The preservation and prosperity of its members. And what is the surest mark of their preservation and prosperity? Their numbers and population. Look nowhere else for this disputed sign. All else being equal, the government under which, without external aids, without naturalization or colonies, the citizens grow and multiply most, is unquestionably the best. The government under which a people wanes and shrinks is the worst. Statisticians, it is up to you to count, to measure, to compare.[1]

the preference for human prosperity. Those countries in which letters and arts have flourished have been too much admired, because the hidden object of their cultivation has not been understood, and their fatal effects not taken into account. “Idque apud imperitos humanitas vocabatur, cum pars servitutis esset.” [“Fools called ‘humanity’ what was a part of slavery,” Tacitus, _Agricola_, 31.] Shall we never see, in the maxims books lay down, the vulgar interest that prompts their writers? No: whatever they say, when, despite its renown, a country is depopulated, it is not true that all is well, and it is not enough that a poet should have an income of 100,000 francs to make his age the best of all. Less attention should be paid to the apparent repose and tranquility of the rulers than to the well-being of their nations as wholes, and above all of the most populous States. A hailstorm lays waste several cantons, but rarely brings on a famine. Outbreaks and civil wars give rulers rude shocks, but they are not the real ills of peoples, who may even get a respite while there is a dispute over who shall tyrannize them. Their true prosperity and calamities come from their permanent condition: it is when the whole remains crushed beneath the yoke that decay sets in, and the rulers destroy the people at will, and “ubi solitudinem faciunt, pacem appellant” [“Where they create a desert, they call it peace,” Tacitus, _Agricola_, 31.] When the squabbles of the great disturbed the kingdom of France, and the Coadjutor of Paris carried a dagger in his pocket to the Parliament, these things did not prevent the people of France from prospering and multiplying in dignity, ease, and freedom. Long ago Greece flourished in the midst of the most savage wars; blood ran in torrents, and yet the whole country was full of inhabitants. It seemed, says Machiavelli, that in the midst of murder, proscription, and civil war, our republic only thrived: the virtue, morality, and independence of the citizens did more to strengthen it than all their dissensions did to weaken it. A little disturbance gives the soul elasticity; what makes the race truly prosperous is not so much peace as liberty.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 10 — The Abuse of Government and Its Tendency to Degenerate
paragraphs: Since the particular will is constantly acting in opposition to the general will, the government continually exerts itself against the Sovereignty. The greater this exertion grows, the more the constitution changes; and since in this case there is no other corporate will to create an equilibrium by resisting the will of the prince, sooner or later the prince must inevitably suppress the Sovereign and break the social treaty. This is the unavoidable and inherent defect that, from the very birth of the body politic, ceaselessly tends to destroy it, just as age and death end by destroying the human body.
There are two general courses by which government degenerates: when it undergoes contraction, or when the State is dissolved.

Government undergoes contraction when it passes from the many to the few — that is, from democracy to aristocracy, and from aristocracy to royalty. This is its natural tendency.[1] If it took the reverse course from the few to the many, it could be said to be loosening; but this inverse sequence is impossible.

Indeed, governments never change their form except when their energy is exhausted and leaves them too weak to keep what they have. If a government simultaneously extended its sphere and slackened its grip, its force would become absolutely zero, and it would last even less time. So the spring must be wound up and the grip tightened as it gives way; otherwise, the State it sustains will come to grief.
The dissolution of the State can happen in either of two ways.

First, when the prince ceases to administer the State in accordance with the laws and usurps the Sovereign power. A remarkable change then occurs: not the government but the State undergoes contraction; I mean that the great State is dissolved, and another is formed within it, made up solely of the members of the government, which becomes for the rest of the people merely master and tyrant. So that the moment the government usurps the Sovereignty, the social compact is broken, and all private citizens recover by right their natural liberty, and are forced — though not bound — to obey.

The same thing happens when the members of the government individually usurp the power they should exercise only as a body. This is just as great an infraction of the laws, and produces even greater disorders. There are then, so to speak, as many princes as there are magistrates, and the State, no less divided than the government, either perishes or changes its form.

When the State is dissolved, the abuse of government, whatever it may be, bears the common name of _anarchy_. To distinguish more carefully: democracy degenerates into _ochlocracy_ and aristocracy into _oligarchy_; and I would add that royalty degenerates into _tyranny_ — but this last word is ambiguous and needs explaining.

In ordinary usage, a tyrant is a king who governs violently and without regard for justice and law. In the strict sense, a tyrant is an individual who arrogates to himself the royal authority without having a right to it. This is how the Greeks understood the word “tyrant”: they applied it indifferently to good and bad princes whose authority was not legitimate.[2] _Tyrant_ and _usurper_ are thus perfect synonyms.

To give different things different names, I call _tyrant_ the man who usurps royal authority, and _despot_ the man who usurps the sovereign power. The tyrant is the one who breaks in, contrary to the laws, in order to govern in accordance with the laws; the despot is the one who sets himself above the laws themselves. Thus the tyrant cannot be a despot, but the despot is always a tyrant.

the Venetian lagoons offer a notable instance of this sequence; and it is most astonishing that, after more than twelve hundred years of existence, the Venetians seem to be still at the second stage, which they reached with the _Serrar di Consiglio_ in 1198. As for the ancient Dukes brought up against them, it is proved — whatever the _Squittinio della libertà veneta_ may say of them — that they were in no sense Sovereigns.

A case sure to be cited against my view is that of the Roman Republic, which, it will be said, followed exactly the opposite course, passing from monarchy to aristocracy and from aristocracy to democracy. I do not at all see it that way.

What Romulus first set up was a mixed government, which soon deteriorated into despotism. From special causes, the State died an untimely death, just as newborn children sometimes perish without reaching manhood. The expulsion of the Tarquins was the real moment of the Republic’s birth. But at first it took on no constant form, because by not abolishing the patriciate, it left half its work undone. By this means, hereditary aristocracy — the worst of all legitimate forms of administration — remained in conflict with democracy, and the form of the government, as Machiavelli has shown, was only fixed with the establishment of the tribunate. Only then was there a true government and a real democracy. In fact, the people was then not only Sovereign but also magistrate and judge; the senate was only a subordinate tribunal, to temper and concentrate the government, and the consuls themselves, though patricians, first magistrates, and absolute generals in war, were in Rome itself nothing more than presidents of the people.

From that point on, the government followed its natural tendency and inclined strongly toward aristocracy. The patriciate, we may say, abolished itself, and the aristocracy was to be found no longer in the body of patricians, as in Venice and Genoa, but in the body of the senate, which was made up of patricians and plebeians, and even in the body of tribunes when they began to usurp an active function: for names do not affect facts, and when the people has rulers who govern for it, whatever name they bear, the government is an aristocracy.

The abuse of aristocracy led to the civil wars and the triumvirate. Sulla, Julius Cæsar, and Augustus became, in fact, real monarchs; and finally, under the despotism of Tiberius, the State was dissolved. Roman history, then, confirms rather than refutes the principle I have laid down.

perpetua in ea civitate quæ libertate usa est (Cornelius Nepos, _Life of Miltiades_). [For all those are called and considered tyrants who hold perpetual power in a State that has known liberty.] It is true that Aristotle (_Nicomachean Ethics_, Book viii, chapter x) distinguishes the tyrant from the king by the fact that the former governs in his own interest and the latter only for the good of his subjects; but not only did all Greek authors generally use the word _tyrant_ in a different sense, as appears most clearly in Xenophon’s _Hiero_, but it would also follow from Aristotle’s distinction that, from the very beginning of the world, there has not yet been a single king.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 11 — The Death of the Body Politic
paragraphs: Such is the natural and inevitable tendency of even the best-constituted governments. If Sparta and Rome perished, what State can hope to last forever? If we want to set up a long-lived form of government, let us not even dream of making it eternal. To succeed, we must not attempt the impossible, or flatter ourselves that we are giving the work of man a stability that human conditions do not allow.

The body politic, like the human body, begins to die as soon as it is born, and carries within itself the causes of its destruction. But each may have a constitution more or less robust, more or less suited to preserving it for a longer or shorter time. Man’s constitution is the work of nature; that of the State is the work of art. It is not in men’s power to prolong their own lives; but it is in their power to prolong the life of the State as much as possible, by giving it the best possible constitution. The best-constituted State will have an end; but it will end later than any other, unless some unforeseen accident brings about its untimely destruction.

The life-principle of the body politic lies in the sovereign authority. The legislative power is the heart of the State; the executive power is its brain, which sets all the parts in motion. The brain may be paralyzed and the individual still live. A man may remain an imbecile and live; but as soon as the heart stops performing its functions, the animal is dead.

The State exists by means not of the laws but of the legislative power. Yesterday’s law is not binding today; but silence is taken for tacit consent, and the Sovereign is held continually to confirm the laws it does not abrogate when it could. Whatever it has once declared itself to will, it wills always, unless it revokes its declaration.

Why, then, is so much respect paid to old laws? For this very reason. We must believe that nothing but the excellence of old acts of will can have preserved them so long: had the Sovereign not recognized them as wholesome throughout, it would have revoked them a thousand times. This is why, far from growing weak, the laws continually gain new strength in any well-constituted State; the precedent of antiquity makes them daily more venerable. Wherever, on the contrary, the laws grow weak as they grow old, this proves that there is no longer a legislative power, and that the State is dead.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 12 — How the Sovereign Authority Maintains Itself
paragraphs: The Sovereign, having no force other than the legislative power, acts only by means of the laws; and since the laws are nothing but the authentic acts of the general will, the Sovereign cannot act except when the people is assembled. The people in assembly, I shall be told, is a mere chimera. It is so today, but two thousand years ago it was not. Has man’s nature changed?

The bounds of possibility, in moral matters, are less narrow than we imagine: it is our weaknesses, our vices, and our prejudices that confine them. Base souls have no belief in great men; vile slaves smile in mockery at the name of liberty.

Let us judge what can be done by what has been done. I shall say nothing of the Republics of ancient Greece; but the Roman Republic was, to my mind, a great State, and the town of Rome a great town. The last census showed that there were in Rome four hundred thousand citizens capable of bearing arms, and the last computation of the population of the Empire showed over four million citizens, excluding subjects, foreigners, women, children, and slaves.

What difficulties might one not suppose stood in the way of the frequent assembling of the vast population of this capital and its neighborhood. Yet few weeks passed without the Roman people being in assembly, and even being so several times. It exercised not only the rights of Sovereignty, but also part of those of government. It dealt with certain matters and judged certain cases, and this entire people was found in the public meeting-place hardly less often as magistrates than as citizens.

If we went back to the earliest history of nations, we would find that most ancient governments — even those of monarchical form, like the Macedonian and the Frankish — had similar councils. In any case, the one incontestable fact I have given is an answer to all difficulties: it is good logic to reason from the actual to the possible.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 13 — The Same (continued)
paragraphs: It is not enough for the assembled people to have once fixed the constitution of the State by giving its sanction to a body of laws; it is not enough for it to have set up a perpetual government, or provided once and for all for the election of magistrates. Beyond the extraordinary assemblies that unforeseen circumstances may demand, there must be fixed periodic assemblies that cannot be canceled or postponed, so that on the appointed day the people is legitimately called together by law, without need of any formal summons.

But aside from these assemblies authorized by their date alone, every assembly of the people not summoned by the magistrates appointed for that purpose, and according to the prescribed forms, must be regarded as unlawful, and all its acts as null and void — because the command to assemble must itself proceed from the law.

How frequently lawful assemblies should occur depends on so many considerations that no exact rules can be given. It can only be said, in general, that the stronger the government, the more often the Sovereign should show itself.

This, I shall be told, may do for a single town; but what is to be done when the State includes several? Is the sovereign authority to be divided? Or is it to be concentrated in a single town to which all the rest are made subject?

Neither the one nor the other, I answer. First, the sovereign authority is one and simple, and cannot be divided without being destroyed. Second, one town can no more legitimately be made subject to another than one nation can — because the essence of the body politic lies in reconciling obedience and liberty, and the words subject and Sovereign are identical correlatives whose idea meets in the single word “citizen.”

I answer further that the union of several towns into a single city is always bad, and that if we want to make such a union, we should not expect to escape its natural disadvantages. It is useless to bring up the abuses peculiar to great States against someone who only wants to see small ones. But how can small States be given the strength to resist great ones, as the Greek towns once resisted the Great King, and as more recently Holland and Switzerland have resisted the House of Austria?

Still, if the State cannot be reduced to the right limits, one resource remains: to allow no capital, to make the seat of government move from town to town, and to assemble in turn in each the Provincial Estates of the country.

People the territory evenly, extend the same rights everywhere, carry abundance and life to every place: by these means the State will become at once as strong and as well-governed as possible. Remember that the walls of towns are built of the ruins of the houses of the countryside. For every palace I see raised in the capital, my mind’s eye sees a whole country laid waste.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 14 — The Same (continued)
paragraphs: The moment the people is legitimately assembled as a sovereign body, the jurisdiction of the government wholly lapses, the executive power is suspended, and the person of the meanest citizen is as sacred and inviolable as that of the first magistrate; for in the presence of the person represented, representatives no longer exist. Most of the tumults that broke out in the comitia at Rome were due to ignorance or neglect of this rule. The consuls in those assemblies were merely presidents of the people; the tribunes were mere speakers;[1] the senate was nothing at all.

These intervals of suspension, during which the prince recognizes — or ought to recognize — an actual superior, have always been viewed by him with alarm; and these assemblies of the people, which are the shield of the body politic and the curb on government, have at all times been the horror of rulers, who therefore spare no efforts, objections, difficulties, or promises in keeping the citizens from holding them. When the citizens are greedy, cowardly, and faint-hearted, and love ease more than liberty, they do not long hold out against the redoubled efforts of the government; and so, as the resisting force constantly grows, the sovereign authority ends by disappearing, and most cities fall and perish before their time.
But between sovereign authority and arbitrary government there sometimes intervenes an intermediate power, of which something must be said.
Parliament. The similarity of these functions would have brought the consuls and the tribunes into conflict, even if all jurisdiction had been suspended.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 15 — Deputies or Representatives
paragraphs: As soon as public service ceases to be the chief business of the citizens, and they would rather serve with their money than with their persons, the State is not far from its fall. When it is necessary to march out to war, they pay troops and stay at home; when it is necessary to meet in council, they appoint deputies and stay at home. Through idleness and money, they end up with soldiers to enslave their country and representatives to sell it.

It is through the bustle of commerce and the arts, through the greedy self-interest of profit, and through softness and love of comforts, that personal service is replaced by money payments. Men give up part of their profits in order to have time to increase them at leisure. Make gifts of money, and you will not long be without chains. The word _finance_ is a slavish word, unknown in the city-state. In a country that is truly free, the citizens do everything with their own arms, and nothing by money; far from paying to be excused from their duties, they would even pay for the privilege of fulfilling them themselves. I am far from taking the common view: I hold forced labor to be less opposed to liberty than taxes.

The better the constitution of a State, the more public affairs encroach on private ones in the minds of the citizens. Private affairs are even of much less importance, because the aggregate of common happiness provides a greater portion of each person’s happiness, leaving less to be sought through individual concerns. In a well-ordered city, every man hurries to the assemblies; under a bad government no one cares to take a step toward them, because no one is interested in what happens there, because it is foreseen that the general will will not prevail, and finally because domestic cares are all-consuming. Good laws lead to making better ones; bad laws bring on worse. As soon as any man says of the affairs of the State, _What does it matter to me?_, the State may be given up for lost.

The cooling of patriotism, the activity of private interest, the vastness of States, conquest, and the abuse of government suggested the device of having deputies or representatives of the people in the national assemblies. These are what, in some countries, men have presumed to call the Third Estate. So the individual interest of two orders is put first and second, and the public interest occupies only the third place.

Sovereignty, for the same reason that makes it inalienable, cannot be represented; it lies essentially in the general will, and a will does not admit of representation: it is either the same, or other; there is no middle possibility. The deputies of the people, then, are not and cannot be its representatives; they are merely its stewards, and can carry through no definitive acts. Every law the people has not ratified in person is null and void — is, in fact, no law. The people of England regards itself as free, but it is grossly mistaken: it is free only during the election of members of parliament. As soon as they are elected, slavery overtakes it, and it is nothing. The use it makes of the brief moments of liberty it enjoys shows that it deserves to lose them.

The idea of representation is modern; it comes to us from feudal government — from that iniquitous and absurd system that degrades humanity and dishonors the name of man. In ancient republics, and even in monarchies, the people never had representatives; the word itself was unknown. It is most striking that in Rome, where the tribunes were so sacrosanct, it was never even imagined that they could usurp the functions of the people, and that in the midst of so vast a multitude they never tried to pass a single plebiscitum on their own authority. We can, however, get an idea of the difficulties caused at times by the people being so numerous, from what happened in the time of the Gracchi, when some of the citizens had to cast their votes from the rooftops of buildings.

Where right and liberty are everything, disadvantages count for nothing. Among this wise people, everything was given its just value; its lictors were allowed to do what its tribunes would never have dared to attempt — for it had no fear that its lictors would try to represent it.

But to explain how the tribunes did sometimes represent the people, it is enough to grasp how the government represents the Sovereign. Since law is purely the declaration of the general will, it is clear that, in the exercise of legislative power, the people cannot be represented; but in the exercise of executive power, which is only the force applied to give the law effect, it both can and should be represented. We thus see that, if we looked closely into the matter, we would find that very few nations have any laws at all. However that may be, it is certain that the tribunes, having no executive power, could never represent the Roman people by right of the powers entrusted to them, but only by usurping those of the senate.

In Greece, all that the people had to do, it did for itself; it was constantly assembled in the public square. The Greeks lived in a mild climate; they had no natural greed; slaves did their work for them; their great concern was liberty. Lacking the same advantages, how can you preserve the same rights? Your harsher climates add to your needs;[1] for half the year your public squares are uninhabitable; the flatness of your languages unfits them for being heard in the open air; you sacrifice more for profit than for liberty, and fear slavery less than poverty.

What, then? Is liberty maintained only with the help of slavery? Perhaps. Extremes meet. Everything that is not in the course of nature has its disadvantages, civil society most of all. There are some unhappy circumstances in which we can keep our liberty only at the expense of others, and where the citizen can be perfectly free only when the slave is most a slave. Such was the case in Sparta. As for you, modern peoples, you have no slaves, but you are slaves yourselves; you pay for their liberty with your own. In vain do you boast of this preference; I find in it more cowardice than humanity.

I do not mean by all this that it is necessary to have slaves, or that the right of slavery is legitimate; I am merely giving the reasons why modern peoples, believing themselves free, have representatives, while ancient peoples had none. In any case, the moment a people allows itself to be represented, it is no longer free: it no longer exists.

All things considered, I do not see how it is possible from now on for the Sovereign to preserve among us the exercise of its rights, unless the city is very small. But if it is very small, will it not be conquered? No. I will show later how the external strength of a great people[2] may be combined with the convenient polity and good order of a small State.
to want to submit to its chains; it is, in fact, to bend to them far more inevitably in our case than in theirs.
in dealing with external relations, I came to the subject of confederations. The subject is quite new, and its principles have still to be laid down.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 16 — That the Institution of Government Is Not a Contract
paragraphs: Once the legislative power has been firmly established, the next thing is to establish the executive power in the same way; for the executive power, which operates only by particular acts, is not of the essence of the legislative, and is naturally separate from it. If it were possible for the Sovereign, as such, to possess the executive power, right and fact would be so confused that no one could tell what was law and what was not; and the body politic, thus disfigured, would soon fall prey to the very violence it was instituted to prevent.

Since the citizens, by the social contract, are all equal, all can prescribe what all should do, but no one has a right to demand that another do what he himself does not. It is precisely this right — indispensable for giving the body politic life and movement — that the Sovereign, in instituting the government, confers upon the prince.

It has been held that this act of establishment was a contract between the people and the rulers it sets over itself — a contract laying down terms binding one side to command and the other to obey. This is, I am sure it will be admitted, an odd kind of contract to enter into. But let us see whether this view can be maintained.

First, the supreme authority can no more be modified than it can be alienated; to limit it is to destroy it. It is absurd and self-contradictory for the Sovereign to set a superior over itself; to bind itself to obey a master would be a return to absolute liberty.

Moreover, it is clear that this contract between the people and certain particular persons would be a particular act; and from this it follows that it can be neither a law nor an act of Sovereignty, and so would be illegitimate.

It is also plain that the contracting parties, in relation to each other, would be under the law of nature alone, with no guarantees of their mutual undertakings — a position completely at odds with the civil state. Since the man who has force at his command is always in a position to control execution, it would come to the same thing if we called a “contract” the act of one man saying to another, “I give you all my goods, on condition that you give me back as much of them as you please.”

There is only one contract in the State — the act of association — and that contract in itself excludes the existence of a second. It is impossible to conceive of any public contract that would not be a violation of the first.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 17 — The Institution of Government
paragraphs: Under what general idea, then, should the act by which government is instituted be conceived as falling? I will begin by stating that the act is complex, being made up of two others — the establishment of the law and its execution.
By the first, the Sovereign decrees that there shall be a governing body established in such-and-such a form; this act is clearly a law.

By the second, the people nominates the rulers who are to be entrusted with the government that has been established. This nomination, being a particular act, is clearly not a second law, but merely a consequence of the first and a function of government.

The difficulty is to understand how there can be a governmental act before government exists, and how the people, being only Sovereign or subject, can, under certain circumstances, become a prince or magistrate.

It is here that one of the astonishing properties of the body politic reveals itself, by which it reconciles apparently contradictory operations. For this is achieved by a sudden conversion of Sovereignty into democracy, so that, without any perceptible change, and merely by virtue of a new relation of all to all, the citizens become magistrates and pass from general to particular acts, from legislation to the execution of the law.

This changed relation is no speculative subtlety without practical instances: it happens every day in the English Parliament, where, on certain occasions, the Lower House resolves itself into Grand Committee, for the better discussion of business, and so, having been at one moment a sovereign court, becomes at the next a mere commission. It then reports back to itself, as House of Commons, the result of its proceedings in Grand Committee, and debates again under one name what it has already settled under another.

It is, indeed, the peculiar advantage of democratic government that it can be established in actuality by a simple act of the general will. Afterward, this provisional government either remains in power, if this form is adopted, or else, in the name of the Sovereign, sets up the government prescribed by law; and so the whole proceeding is regular. It is impossible to set up government in any other way legitimately, and in accordance with the principles laid down so far.

chapters.title: Book 3, Chapter 18 — How to Check the Usurpations of Government
paragraphs: What we have just said confirms Chapter XVI, and makes it clear that the institution of government is not a contract but a law; that the trustees of executive power are not the people’s masters but its officers; that it can set them up and pull them down as it pleases; that for them there is no question of contract, but of obedience; and that, in taking on the functions the State imposes upon them, they are doing no more than fulfilling their duty as citizens, without any right to argue about the conditions.

So when the people sets up a hereditary government — whether monarchical and confined to one family, or aristocratic and confined to a class — what it enters into is not an undertaking; the administration is given a provisional form, until the people chooses to order it otherwise.

It is true that such changes are always dangerous, and that the established government should never be touched unless it becomes incompatible with the public good; but the caution this involves is a maxim of policy, not a rule of right, and the State is no more bound to leave civil authority in the hands of its rulers than it is to leave military authority in the hands of its generals.

It is also true that, in such cases, one cannot be too careful to observe all the formalities required to distinguish a regular and legitimate act from a seditious tumult, and the will of a whole people from the clamor of a faction. Here above all, no further concession should be made to the awkward possibility than cannot, in the strictest logic, be refused. From this obligation the prince derives a great advantage in keeping his power against the people, without anyone being able to say he has usurped it. Seeming to avail himself only of his rights, he finds it very easy to extend them, and to prevent — under the pretext of keeping the peace — assemblies whose purpose is to re-establish order. Thus he takes advantage of a silence he does not allow to be broken, or of irregularities he himself causes, to assume that he has the support of those whom fear keeps from speaking, and to punish those who dare to speak. So it was that the decemvirs, first elected for one year and then kept on for a second, tried to perpetuate their power by forbidding the comitia to assemble. By this easy method, every government in the world, once clothed in public power, sooner or later usurps the sovereign authority.

The periodic assemblies I have already mentioned are designed to prevent or postpone this calamity, especially when they need no formal summons; for in that case, the prince cannot stop them without openly declaring himself a lawbreaker and an enemy of the State.

The opening of these assemblies, whose sole object is the maintenance of the social treaty, should always take the form of putting two propositions, which may not be suppressed, and which should be voted on separately.
The first is: “Does it please the Sovereign to preserve the present form of government?”
The second is: “Does it please the people to leave its administration in the hands of those who are actually in charge of it?”

I am here assuming what I think I have shown — that there is in the State no fundamental law that cannot be revoked, not excluding the social compact itself; for if all the citizens assembled with one accord to break the compact, it is impossible to doubt that it would be very legitimately broken. Grotius even thinks that each man can renounce his membership of his own State and recover his natural liberty and his goods on leaving the country.[1] It would indeed be absurd if all the citizens in assembly could not do what each can do by himself.
and avoid having to serve his country in the hour of need. Flight in such a case would be criminal and punishable, and would be not withdrawal but desertion.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 1 — That the General Will Is Indestructible
paragraphs: As long as several men in assembly regard themselves as a single body, they have only a single will, concerned with their common preservation and general well-being. In this case, all the springs of the State are vigorous and simple, and its rules clear and luminous; there are no entanglements or conflicts of interest; the common good is everywhere plainly visible, and only good sense is needed to see it. Peace, unity, and equality are the enemies of political subtleties. Men who are upright and simple are hard to deceive precisely because of their simplicity; lures and ingenious pretexts fail to take them in, and they are not even cunning enough to be dupes. When, among the happiest people in the world, bands of peasants are seen regulating affairs of State under an oak, and always acting wisely, can we help despising the elaborate methods of other nations, which make themselves illustrious and miserable with so much art and mystery?

A State so governed needs very few laws; and when new ones become necessary, the necessity is universally seen. The first man to propose them merely says what everyone has already felt, and there is no question of factions, intrigues, or eloquence to push into law what each has already decided to do, as soon as he is sure the rest will join him.

Theorists are led astray because, seeing only States that have been wrongly constituted from the start, they are struck by the impossibility of applying such a policy to them. They make great sport of all the absurdities that a clever rascal or an insinuating speaker might persuade the people of Paris or London to believe. They do not realize that Cromwell would have been put to “the bells” by the people of Berne, and the Duc de Beaufort on the treadmill by the Genevese.

But when the social bond begins to loosen and the State to grow weak, when particular interests begin to make themselves felt and the smaller societies start to influence the larger, the common interest changes and meets opponents; opinion is no longer unanimous; the general will ceases to be the will of all; contradictory views and debates arise; and the best advice is no longer accepted without question.

Finally, when the State, on the brink of ruin, maintains only a vain, illusory, and formal existence, when in every heart the social bond is broken, and the meanest interest brazenly seizes the sacred name of “public good,” the general will falls silent. All men, guided by secret motives, no more give their views as citizens than if the State had never existed; and iniquitous decrees, aimed solely at private interest, are passed under the name of laws.

Does it follow that the general will has been wiped out or corrupted? Not at all: it is always constant, unalterable, and pure; but it is subordinated to other wills that encroach on its sphere. Each man, in detaching his interest from the common interest, sees clearly that he cannot entirely separate them; but his share in the public misfortunes seems negligible to him beside the exclusive good he aims at making his own. Apart from this particular good, he wills the general good in his own interest as strongly as anyone else. Even in selling his vote for money, he does not extinguish the general will in himself — he only evades it. The fault he commits is changing the question, and answering something different from what he is asked. Instead of saying, by his vote, “It is to the State’s advantage,” he says, “It is to this or that man’s or party’s advantage that this or that view should prevail.” So the law of public order in assemblies is not so much to maintain the general will in them as to ensure that the question is always put to it, and the answer always given by it.

I could here set down many reflections on the simple right of voting in every act of Sovereignty — a right no one can take from the citizens — and also on the right to state views, make proposals, divide and discuss, which the government is always most careful to leave only to its own members; but this important subject would need a treatise of its own, and one cannot say everything in a single work.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 2 — Voting
paragraphs: It can be seen, from the last chapter, that the way general business is managed gives a clear enough indication of the actual state of morals and the health of the body politic. The more concert reigns in the assemblies — that is, the closer opinion comes to unanimity — the greater is the dominance of the general will. On the other hand, long debates, dissensions, and tumult announce the ascendancy of particular interests and the decline of the State.

This seems less clear when two or more orders enter into the constitution, as patricians and plebeians did at Rome; for quarrels between these two orders often disturbed the comitia, even in the best days of the Republic. But the exception is more apparent than real; for then, through the defect inherent in that body politic, there were, so to speak, two States in one, and what is not true of the two together is true of either separately. Even in the most stormy times, the plebiscita of the people, when the Senate did not interfere, always went through quietly and by large majorities. Since the citizens had only one interest, the people had only a single will.

At the other extremity of the circle, unanimity returns; this is the case when the citizens, having fallen into servitude, have lost both liberty and will. Fear and flattery then turn votes into acclamations; deliberation ceases, and only worship or curses remain. Such was the vile manner in which the senate expressed its views under the Emperors. They sometimes did so with absurd precautions. Tacitus observes that under Otho the senators, while heaping curses on Vitellius, contrived at the same time to make a deafening noise, so that, should he ever become their master, he might not know what each of them had said.

On these various considerations depend the rules by which the methods of counting votes and comparing opinions should be regulated, according to whether the general will is more or less easy to discover, and the State is more or less in decline.

There is only one law that, by its nature, requires unanimous consent. This is the social compact; for civil association is the most voluntary of all acts. Since every man is born free and his own master, no one, under any pretext whatsoever, can make any man subject without his consent. To decide that the son of a slave is born a slave is to decide that he is not born a man.

If, then, there are opponents when the social compact is made, their opposition does not invalidate the contract, but merely keeps them from being included in it. They are foreigners among citizens. Once the State is instituted, residence implies consent: to live within its territory is to submit to the Sovereign.[1]

Apart from this primitive contract, the vote of the majority always binds all the rest. This follows from the contract itself. But it is asked how a man can be both free and forced to conform to wills that are not his own. How are the opponents at once free and subject to laws they have not agreed to?

I answer that the question is wrongly put. The citizen consents to all the laws, including those passed in spite of his opposition, and even those that punish him when he dares to break any of them. The constant will of all the members of the State is the general will; by virtue of it they are citizens and free.[2] When a law is proposed in the popular assembly, what the people is asked is not exactly whether they approve or reject the proposal, but whether it is in conformity with the general will, which is their will. Each man, in giving his vote, states his opinion on that point; and the general will is found by counting votes. So when the opinion contrary to my own prevails, this proves no more and no less than that I was mistaken, and that what I thought was the general will was not. If my particular opinion had carried the day, I would have done the opposite of what I willed — and it is in that case that I would not have been free.
This presupposes, of course, that all the qualities of the general will still reside in the majority: when they no longer do, then whatever side a man may take, liberty is no longer possible.

In my earlier demonstration of how particular wills are substituted for the general will in public deliberation, I have already pointed out the practical methods of avoiding this abuse; and I shall have more to say about them later. I have also given the principles for determining the proportional number of votes needed to declare that will. A difference of one vote destroys equality; a single opponent destroys unanimity; but between equality and unanimity there are several grades of unequal division, at each of which this proportion can be fixed according to the condition and needs of the body politic.

There are two general rules that may serve to regulate this relation. First, the more grave and important the matters discussed, the closer the prevailing opinion should come to unanimity. Second, the more the matter at hand calls for speed, the smaller the prescribed difference in the number of votes may be allowed to become; where an instant decision must be reached, a majority of one vote should be enough. The first of these two rules seems more in line with the laws, the second more with practical affairs. In any case, it is the combination of them that gives the best proportions for determining the necessary majority.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 3 — Elections
paragraphs: In the elections of the prince and the magistrates — which, as I have said, are complex acts — there are two possible methods: choice and lot. Both have been used in various republics, and a highly complicated mixture of the two still survives in the election of the Doge at Venice.

“Election by lot,” says Montesquieu, “is democratic in nature.” I agree that it is; but in what sense? “The lot,” he goes on, “is a way of making a choice that is unfair to no one; it leaves each citizen a reasonable hope of serving his country.” These are not reasons.

If we keep in mind that the election of rulers is a function of government and not of Sovereignty, we will see why the lot is the method more natural to democracy, in which the administration is better the smaller the number of its acts.

In every real democracy, magistracy is not an advantage but a burdensome charge that cannot justly be imposed on one individual rather than another. Only the law can place it on the man on whom the lot falls. For, the conditions then being the same for all, and the choice not depending on any human will, there is no particular application that alters the universality of the law.
In an aristocracy, the prince chooses the prince, the government is preserved by itself, and voting is rightly ordered.

The example of the election of the Doge of Venice confirms this distinction rather than destroying it; the mixed form suits a mixed government. For it is a mistake to take the government of Venice for a real aristocracy. If the people has no share in the government, the nobility is itself the people. A host of poor Barnabotes never gets near any magistracy, and its nobility consists merely in the empty title of Excellency, and in the right to sit in the Great Council. Since this Great Council is as numerous as our General Council at Geneva, its illustrious members have no more privileges than our plain citizens. It is undeniable that, apart from the extreme disparity between the two republics, the _bourgeoisie_ of Geneva is exactly equivalent to the _patriciate_ of Venice; our _natives_ and _inhabitants_ correspond to the _townsmen_ and _people_ of Venice; our _peasants_ correspond to the _subjects_ on the mainland; and however that republic may be regarded, if its size is left out of account, its government is no more aristocratic than our own. The whole difference is that, having no life-ruler, we do not, like Venice, need to use the lot.

Election by lot would have few disadvantages in a real democracy in which, since equality would prevail everywhere — in morals and talents as well as in principles and fortunes — it would become almost a matter of indifference who was chosen. But I have already said that a real democracy is only an ideal.

When choice and lot are combined, posts requiring special talents, such as military positions, should be filled by the former; the latter does for cases — such as judicial offices — in which good sense, justice, and integrity are enough, because in a well-constituted State these qualities are common to all the citizens.

Neither lot nor vote has any place in monarchical government. The monarch being by right sole prince and only magistrate, the choice of his lieutenants belongs to him alone. When the Abbé de Saint-Pierre proposed that the Councils of the King of France should be multiplied and their members elected by ballot, he did not see that he was proposing to change the form of government.

I should now speak of the methods of giving and counting opinions in the assembly of the people; but perhaps an account of this aspect of the Roman constitution will more forcibly illustrate all the rules I could lay down. It is worth the trouble of a thoughtful reader to follow in some detail the working of public and private affairs in a Council of two hundred thousand men.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 4 — The Roman Comitia
paragraphs: We have no well-certified records of the first period of Rome’s existence; it even seems very probable that most of the stories told about it are fables. In general, the most instructive part of the history of any people — that which deals with its founding — is what we have least of. Experience teaches us every day what causes lead to the revolutions of empires; but, since no new peoples are now formed, we have almost nothing but conjecture to go on in explaining how they were created.

The customs we find established show at least that those customs had an origin. The traditions that go back to those origins, that have the greatest authorities behind them, and that are confirmed by the strongest proofs, should pass for the most certain. These are the rules I have tried to follow in inquiring how the freest and most powerful people on earth exercised its supreme power.

After the founding of Rome, the newborn republic — that is, the army of its founder, made up of Albans, Sabines, and foreigners — was divided into three classes, which from this division took the name of _tribes_. Each of these tribes was subdivided into ten _curiæ_, and each _curia_ into _decuriæ_, headed by leaders called _curiones_ and _decuriones_.

Besides this, out of each tribe was drawn a body of one hundred _Equites_, or Knights, called a _century_, which shows that these divisions, being unnecessary in a town, were at first merely military. But an instinct for greatness seems to have led the little township of Rome to provide itself in advance with a political system suitable for the capital of the world.

An awkward situation soon arose from this original division. The tribes of the Albans (Ramnenses) and the Sabines (Tatienses) remained always in the same condition, while that of the foreigners (Luceres) continually grew, as more and more foreigners came to live at Rome, so that it soon outstripped the others in strength. Servius remedied this dangerous defect by changing the principle of division, abolishing the racial division and replacing it with one based on the quarter of the town inhabited by each tribe. Instead of three tribes he created four, each occupying and named after one of the hills of Rome. So while redressing the inequality of the moment, he also provided for the future; and to make the division one of persons as well as of places, he forbade the inhabitants of one quarter to migrate to another, and so prevented the mingling of the races.

He also doubled the three old centuries of Knights and added twelve more, still keeping the old names; by this simple and prudent method, he managed to distinguish the body of Knights from the people without a murmur from the latter.

To the four urban tribes Servius added fifteen others called rural tribes, because they were made up of country dwellers, divided into fifteen cantons. Later, fifteen more were created, and the Roman people finally found itself divided into thirty-five tribes — as it remained down to the end of the Republic.

The distinction between urban and rural tribes had one effect worth mentioning, both because it has no parallel elsewhere, and because it was to it that Rome owed the preservation of her morality and the enlargement of her empire. We would have expected that the urban tribes would soon monopolize power and honors, and lose no time in bringing the rural tribes into disrepute; but exactly the reverse happened. The taste of the early Romans for country life is well known. They owed it to their wise founder, who tied rural and military labors to liberty, and, so to speak, banished to the town the arts, crafts, intrigue, fortune, and slavery.

Since all of Rome’s most illustrious citizens lived in the fields and tilled the earth, men grew used to looking there alone for the mainstays of the republic. This way of life, being that of the best patricians, was honored by all; the simple, laborious life of the villager was preferred to the slothful and idle life of the _bourgeoisie_ of Rome; and a man who, in the town, would have been only a wretched proletarian became, as a laborer in the fields, a respected citizen. Not without reason, says Varro, did our great-souled ancestors set up in the village the nursery of those sturdy and valiant men who defended them in time of war and provided their sustenance in time of peace. Pliny states positively that the country tribes were honored because of the men who composed them; while cowards whom men wished to disgrace were transferred, as a public dishonor, to the town tribes. The Sabine Appius Claudius, when he came to settle in Rome, was loaded with honors and enrolled in a rural tribe, which afterwards took his family name. Lastly, freedmen always entered the urban tribes, never the rural; nor is there a single instance, throughout the Republic, of a freedman, though he had become a citizen, reaching any magistracy.
This was an excellent rule; but it was carried so far that in the end it led to a change, and certainly to an abuse, in the political system.

First, the censors, after long claiming the right to transfer citizens arbitrarily from one tribe to another, eventually allowed most people to enroll themselves in whatever tribe they pleased. This permission certainly did no good, and further deprived the censorship of one of its greatest resources. Moreover, since the great and powerful all got themselves enrolled in the country tribes, while the freedmen who had become citizens stayed with the populace in the town tribes, both soon ceased to have any local or territorial meaning, and all became so confused that the members of one could not be told from those of another except by the registers. So the idea of the word _tribe_ became personal instead of real, or rather came to be little more than a fiction.
It also happened that the town tribes, being more on the spot, were often the stronger in the comitia, and sold the State to those who stooped to buy the votes of the rabble that composed them.

Since the founder had set up ten _curiæ_ in each tribe, the entire Roman people, which was then contained within the walls, consisted of thirty _curiæ_, each with its temples, gods, officers, priests, and festivals — called _compitalia_, and corresponding to the _paganalia_ later held by the rural tribes.

When Servius made his new division, since the thirty _curiæ_ could not be shared equally between his four tribes, and since he was unwilling to interfere with them, they became a further division of the inhabitants of Rome, quite independent of the tribes. But in the case of the rural tribes and their members, there was no question of _curiæ_, since the tribes had by then become a purely civil institution, and a new system of levying troops had been introduced, making the military divisions of Romulus superfluous. So although every citizen was enrolled in a tribe, very many were not members of a _curia_.

Servius made yet a third division, quite distinct from the two we have mentioned, which became, in its effects, the most important of all. He distributed the whole Roman people into six classes, distinguished neither by place nor by person but by wealth. The first classes included the rich, the last the poor, and those between, persons of moderate means. These six classes were subdivided into one hundred and ninety-three other bodies, called centuries, distributed in such a way that the first class alone comprised more than half of them, while the last comprised only one. Thus the class with the smallest number of members had the largest number of centuries, and the entire last class counted as a single subdivision, although it alone included more than half the inhabitants of Rome.

So that the people would have less insight into the results of this arrangement, Servius tried to give it a military tone: into the second class he inserted two centuries of armorers, and into the fourth two of makers of war instruments. In each class except the last, he distinguished young from old — that is, those obliged to bear arms from those whose age gave them legal exemption. It was this distinction, rather than that of wealth, that required frequent repetition of the census or counting. Lastly, he ordered that the assembly should be held in the Campus Martius, and that all those of age to serve should come there armed.

The reason he did not also divide the last class into young and old was that the populace, of whom it was composed, was not granted the right to bear arms for its country: a man had to possess a hearth in order to acquire the right to defend it; and of all the troops of beggars who today lend luster to the armies of kings, there is perhaps not one who would not have been driven out of a Roman cohort with scorn, in the days when soldiers were the defenders of liberty.

In this last class, however, _proletarians_ were distinguished from _capite censi_. The first, not quite reduced to nothing, at least gave the State citizens, and sometimes, when need pressed, even soldiers. Those who had nothing at all, and could be numbered only by counting heads, were regarded as of absolutely no account, and Marius was the first to stoop to enroll them.

Without deciding here whether this third arrangement was good or bad in itself, I think I may state that only the simple morals, the disinterestedness, the liking for agriculture, and the scorn for commerce and the love of gain that characterized the early Romans could have made it workable. Where is the modern people among whom consuming greed, unrest, intrigue, continual relocations, and perpetual changes of fortune would let such a system last twenty years without turning the State upside down? We must indeed observe that morality and the censorship, being stronger than this institution, corrected its defects at Rome, and that the rich man found himself demoted to the class of the poor for making too much display of his riches.

From all this it is easy to understand why only five classes are almost always mentioned, even though there were really six. The sixth, providing neither soldiers to the army nor votes in the Campus Martius,[1] and being almost without function in the State, was rarely regarded as of any account.

These were the various ways in which the Roman people was divided. Let us now see the effect on the assemblies. When lawfully summoned, these were called _comitia_; they were usually held in the public square at Rome or in the Campus Martius, and were distinguished as _Comitia Curiata_, _Comitia Centuriata_, and _Comitia Tributa_, according to the form under which they were convoked. The _Comitia Curiata_ were founded by Romulus, the _Centuriata_ by Servius, and the _Tributa_ by the tribunes of the people. No law received its sanction and no magistrate was elected except in the comitia; and since every citizen was enrolled in a _curia_, a century, or a tribe, it follows that no citizen was excluded from the right of voting, and that the Roman people was truly sovereign both _de jure_ and _de facto_.

For the comitia to be lawfully assembled, and for their acts to have the force of law, three conditions were required. First, the body or magistrate convoking them had to possess the necessary authority; second, the assembly had to be held on a day allowed by law; and third, the auguries had to be favorable.

The reason for the first regulation needs no explanation; the second is a matter of policy. The comitia could not be held on festivals or market-days, when the country folk, coming to Rome on business, had no time to spend the day in the public square. By means of the third, the senate held in check the proud and restive people, and properly restrained the ardor of seditious tribunes — who, however, found more than one way of getting around this hindrance.

Laws and the election of rulers were not the only questions submitted to the judgment of the comitia: since the Roman people had taken on itself the most important functions of government, it may be said that the fate of Europe was decided in its assemblies. The variety of their objects gave rise to the various forms these took, depending on the matters they had to pronounce on.

To judge of these various forms, it is enough to compare them. Romulus, when he set up the _curiæ_, had in view the checking of the senate by the people, and of the people by the senate, while maintaining his ascendancy over both alike. He therefore gave the people, by means of this assembly, all the authority of numbers to balance that of power and riches, which he left to the patricians. But, in keeping with the spirit of monarchy, he still gave the patricians the greater advantage in the influence of their clients on the majority of votes. This excellent institution of patron and client was a masterpiece of statesmanship and humanity, without which the patriciate, being flagrantly at odds with the republican spirit, could not have survived. Rome alone has the honor of having given the world this great example, which never led to abuse, and yet has never been imitated.

Since the assemblies by _curiæ_ persisted under the kings up to the time of Servius, and the reign of the later Tarquin was not regarded as legitimate, royal laws were generally called _leges curiatæ_.

Under the Republic, the _curiæ_, still confined to the four urban tribes and including only the populace of Rome, suited neither the senate, which led the patricians, nor the tribunes, who, though plebeians, headed the well-to-do citizens. They therefore fell into disrepute, and their degradation was such that thirty lictors used to assemble and do what the _Comitia Curiata_ should have done.

The division by centuries was so favorable to the aristocracy that it is hard to see at first how the senate ever failed to carry the day in the comitia bearing their name, in which the consuls, the censors, and the other curule magistrates were elected. Indeed, of the one hundred and ninety-three centuries into which the six classes of the whole Roman people were divided, the first class contained ninety-eight; and since voting went solely by centuries, this class alone had a majority over all the rest. When all these centuries agreed, the rest of the votes were not even taken; the decision of the smallest number passed for that of the multitude, and it can be said that, in the _Comitia Centuriata_, decisions were determined far more by the depth of purses than by the number of votes.

But this extreme authority was modified in two ways. First, the tribunes as a rule, and always a great number of plebeians, belonged to the class of the rich, and so counterbalanced the influence of the patricians in the first class.

The second way was this. Instead of having the centuries vote in their fixed order — which would have meant always beginning with the first — the Romans always chose one by lot, which proceeded alone to the election; after this, all the centuries were summoned another day according to their rank, and the same election was repeated, and as a rule confirmed. Thus the authority of example was taken away from rank and given to the lot, on a democratic principle.

From this custom resulted a further advantage. The citizens from the country had time, between the two elections, to inform themselves of the merits of the candidate provisionally nominated, and so did not have to vote without knowing the case. But, on the pretext of speeding things up, this custom was eventually abolished, and both elections were held on the same day.

The _Comitia Tributa_ were properly the council of the Roman people. They were convoked by the tribunes alone; in them the tribunes were elected and passed their plebiscita. The senate not only had no standing in them, but no right even to be present; and the senators, being forced to obey laws on which they could not vote, were in this respect less free than the meanest citizens. This injustice was altogether ill-conceived, and was alone enough to invalidate the decrees of a body to which all its members were not admitted. Had all the patricians attended the comitia by virtue of the right they had as citizens, they would not, as mere private individuals, have had any considerable influence on a vote counted by heads, where the meanest proletarian was as good as the _princeps senatus_.

It can be seen, then, that beyond the order achieved by these various ways of distributing so great a people and taking its votes, the various methods were not just indifferent forms; the results of each were related to the objects that caused it to be preferred.

Without going further into details here, we may gather from what has been said above that the _Comitia Tributa_ were the most favorable to popular government, and the _Comitia Centuriata_ to aristocracy. The _Comitia Curiata_, in which the populace of Rome formed the majority, being fitted only to further tyranny and evil designs, naturally fell into disrepute, and even seditious persons abstained from using a method that revealed their schemes too clearly. It is undeniable that the whole majesty of the Roman people lay solely in the _Comitia Centuriata_, which alone included all; for the _Comitia Curiata_ excluded the rural tribes, and the _Comitia Tributa_ the senate and the patricians.

As for the method of taking the vote, it was, among the ancient Romans, as simple as their morals, though not so simple as at Sparta. Each man declared his vote aloud, and a clerk duly wrote it down; the majority in each tribe determined the vote of the tribe, the majority of the tribes that of the people, and so on with _curiæ_ and centuries. This custom was good as long as honesty prevailed among the citizens, and each man was ashamed to vote publicly in favor of an unjust proposal or an unworthy candidate; but when the people grew corrupt and votes were bought, it was fitting that voting should be secret, in order that purchasers might be restrained by mistrust, and rogues given the means of not being traitors.

I know that Cicero attacks this change, and partly attributes the ruin of the Republic to it. But though I feel the weight Cicero’s authority must carry on such a point, I cannot agree with him; on the contrary, I hold that, for want of enough such changes, the destruction of the State must be hastened. Just as the regimen of the healthy does not suit the sick, we should not try to govern a people that has been corrupted by the laws a good people requires. There is no better proof of this rule than the long life of the Republic of Venice, of which the shadow still exists, solely because its laws are suitable only for wicked men.

The citizens were therefore provided with tablets, by means of which each man could vote without anyone knowing how he voted; new methods were also introduced for collecting the tablets, counting voices, comparing numbers, and so on. But all these precautions did not prevent the good faith of the officers in charge of these tasks[2] from often being suspect. Finally, to prevent intrigues and trafficking in votes, edicts were issued — but their very number proves how useless they were.

Toward the close of the Republic, it was often necessary to resort to extraordinary expedients to make up for the inadequacy of the laws. Sometimes miracles were claimed; but this method, while it might impose on the people, could not impose on those who governed. Sometimes an assembly was hastily called together before the candidates had time to form their factions; sometimes a whole sitting was taken up with talk, when it was seen that the people had been won over and was on the point of taking up a wrong position. But in the end, ambition eluded all attempts to check it; and the most incredible fact of all is that, in the midst of all these abuses, the vast people, thanks to its ancient regulations, never ceased to elect magistrates, pass laws, judge cases, and carry through both public and private business almost as easily as the senate itself could have done.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 5 — The Tribunate
paragraphs: When an exact proportion cannot be established between the constituent parts of the State, or when causes that cannot be removed continually alter the relation of one part to another, recourse is had to the institution of a peculiar magistracy that forms no corporate unity with the rest. This restores to each term its right relation to the others, and provides a link or middle term between either prince and people, or prince and Sovereign, or, if necessary, both at once.

This body, which I shall call the _tribunate_, is the preserver of the laws and of the legislative power. It serves sometimes to protect the Sovereign against the government, as the tribunes of the people did at Rome; sometimes to uphold the government against the people, as the Council of Ten now does at Venice; and sometimes to maintain the balance between the two, as the Ephors did at Sparta.

The tribunate is not a constituent part of the city, and should have no share in either legislative or executive power; but this very fact makes its own power the greater. While it can do nothing, it can prevent anything from being done. It is more sacred and more revered, as the defender of the laws, than the prince who executes them, or the Sovereign who ordains them. This was seen very clearly at Rome, when the proud patricians, for all their scorn of the people, were forced to bow before one of its officers, who had neither auspices nor jurisdiction.

The tribunate, wisely tempered, is the strongest support a good constitution can have. But if its strength is even slightly excessive, it upsets the whole State. Weakness, on the other hand, is not natural to it: provided it is anything at all, it is never less than it should be.

It degenerates into tyranny when it usurps the executive power, which it should confine itself to restraining, and when it tries to dispense with the laws, which it should confine itself to protecting. The immense power of the Ephors, harmless as long as Sparta preserved its morality, hastened corruption once corruption had set in. The blood of Agis, slaughtered by these tyrants, was avenged by his successor; the crime and punishment of the Ephors alike hastened the destruction of the republic, and after Cleomenes Sparta ceased to be of any account. Rome perished in the same way: the excessive power of the tribunes, which they had usurped by degrees, finally served — with the help of laws made to secure liberty — as a safeguard for the emperors who destroyed it. As for the Venetian Council of Ten, it is a tribunal of blood, an object of horror to patricians and people alike; far from giving lofty protection to the laws, it does nothing — now that the laws have been degraded — but strike in the dark blows that no one dares notice.

The tribunate, like the government, grows weak as the number of its members increases. When the tribunes of the Roman people, who first numbered only two and then five, wished to double that number, the senate let them do so, confident that it could use one to check another, as it indeed did afterwards.

The best method of preventing usurpations by so formidable a body — though no government has yet made use of it — would be not to make it permanent, but to set the periods during which it should remain in abeyance. These intervals, which should not be long enough to give abuses time to take hold, can be fixed by law in a way that allows them to be easily shortened at need by extraordinary commissions.

This method seems to me to have no disadvantages, because, as I have said, the tribunate, forming no part of the constitution, can be removed without affecting it. It also seems to be effective, because a newly restored magistrate begins not with the power his predecessor exercised, but with the power the law allows him.

chapters.title: Book 4, Chapter 6 — The Dictatorship
paragraphs: The inflexibility of the laws, which keeps them from adapting to circumstances, may, in certain cases, make them disastrous, and even bring about, at a moment of crisis, the ruin of the State. The order and slowness of the forms they require take time that circumstances sometimes refuse to grant. A thousand cases the legislator has not provided for may arise, and it is a highly necessary part of foresight to recognize that not everything can be foreseen.
It is therefore wrong to wish to make political institutions so strong as to make it impossible to suspend their operation. Even Sparta let its laws lapse.

However, only the greatest dangers can outweigh that of disturbing public order, and the sacred power of the laws should never be halted unless the country’s very existence is at stake. In these rare and obvious cases, provision is made for public security by a particular act entrusting it to the man most worthy of it. This commitment can be carried out in either of two ways, depending on the nature of the danger.

If increasing the activity of the government is a sufficient remedy, power is concentrated in the hands of one or two of its members. In this case the change is not in the authority of the laws, but only in the form of administering them. If, on the other hand, the danger is such that the apparatus of the laws is itself an obstacle to their own preservation, the method is to nominate a supreme ruler who shall silence all the laws and suspend, for a moment, the sovereign authority. In such a case, there is no doubt about the general will, and it is clear that the people’s first intention is that the State should not perish. So suspending the legislative authority is in no way abolishing it; the magistrate who silences it cannot make it speak; he dominates it, but cannot represent it. He can do anything, except make laws.

The first method was used by the Roman senate when, in a consecrated formula, it charged the consuls to provide for the safety of the Republic. The second was used when one of the two consuls nominated a dictator:[1] a custom Rome borrowed from Alba.

During the early period of the Republic, dictatorship was very often resorted to, because the State did not yet have a firm enough basis to maintain itself by the strength of its constitution alone. Since the state of morality at the time made superfluous many precautions necessary in other ages, there was no fear that a dictator would abuse his authority, or try to keep it past his term of office. On the contrary, so much power seemed burdensome to the man invested with it, and he made all speed to lay it down — as if taking the place of the laws had been too troublesome and too dangerous a position to hold.

It is therefore the danger not of its abuse but of its cheapening that makes me criticize the indiscreet use of this supreme magistracy in the earliest times. As long as it was freely used at elections, dedications, and purely formal functions, there was a danger of its becoming less formidable in time of need, and of men coming to regard as empty a title used only on occasions of empty ceremony.

Toward the end of the Republic, the Romans, having grown more cautious, were as unreasonably sparing in their use of the dictatorship as they had once been lavish. It is easy to see that their fears had no foundation: the weakness of the capital protected it against the magistrates within it; a dictator might, in certain cases, defend public liberty, but could never endanger it; and the chains of Rome would be forged not in Rome itself but in her armies. The weak resistance offered by Marius to Sulla, and by Pompey to Cæsar, clearly showed what was to be expected from authority at home against force from abroad.

This misconception led the Romans into great mistakes — for example, the failure to nominate a dictator during the Catilinarian conspiracy. Since only the city itself, with at most some province in Italy, was concerned, the unlimited authority the laws gave to the dictator would have enabled him to make short work of the conspiracy, which was, in fact, stifled only by a combination of lucky chances that human prudence had no right to expect.

Instead, the senate contented itself with entrusting its whole power to the consuls, so that Cicero, in order to take effective action, was forced on a capital point to exceed his powers; and if, in the first transports of joy, his conduct was approved, he was justly called to account later for the blood of citizens spilled in violation of the laws. Such a reproach could never have been leveled at a dictator. But the consul’s eloquence carried the day; and he himself, Roman though he was, loved his own glory better than his country, and sought not so much the most lawful and secure means of saving the State as the means of getting for himself the whole honor of having done so.[2] He was therefore justly honored as the liberator of Rome, and just as justly punished as a lawbreaker. However brilliant his recall may have been, it was undoubtedly an act of pardon.

However this important trust is conferred, it is essential that its duration be fixed at a very brief period, incapable of being extended. In the crises that lead to its adoption, the State is either soon lost or soon saved; and once the immediate need has passed, the dictatorship becomes either tyrannical or pointless. At Rome, where dictators held office for six months only, most of them abdicated before their time was up. Had their term been longer, they might well have tried to extend it further, as the decemvirs did when chosen for a year. The dictator had only time to provide against the need for which he had been chosen; he had no time to think of further projects.
